kana: しゅうでんだいじょうぶ？
english: are you okay for the last train?
use: Asked late in the evening so nobody gets stranded; answer with your cut-off, e.g. 'juuichiji made daijoubu'.

example.romaji: Mou juuji sugiteru kedo, shuuden daijoubu?
example.ja: もう10時過ぎてるけど、終電大丈夫？
example.english: It's past ten. Are you okay for the last train?

examplePolite.romaji: Sorosoro jikan desu kedo, shuuden daijoubu desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: そろそろ時間ですけど、終電大丈夫ですか？
examplePolite.english: It's getting late. Will you make the last train?

notes: Shuuden = the last train of the night; missing it means a taxi, a karaoke booth or an all-nighter.

english: sorry for the trouble; thanks, I owe you
use: Said to a friend who does you a favour or goes out of their way, mixing thanks with apology; they answer 'ii yo, ii yo'.

example.romaji: Ogotte moratte warui ne.
example.ja: おごってもらって悪いね。
example.english: Thanks for treating me. I owe you.

examplePolite.romaji: Iroiro tetsudatte moratte, sumimasen.
examplePolite.ja: いろいろ手伝ってもらって、すみません。
examplePolite.english: Thanks for all your help, and sorry for the trouble.

notes: More common from men and older speakers; 'gomen ne, arigatou' does the same job.

english: it was my fault; my bad
use: A sincere apology that takes the blame, usually after an argument; often paired with 'gomen'.

example.romaji: Gomen, watashi ga warukatta. Mou shinai.
example.ja: ごめん、私が悪かった。もうしない。
example.english: Sorry, it was my fault. I won't do it again.

examplePolite.romaji: Kono ken wa watashi ga warukatta desu. Sumimasen.
examplePolite.ja: この件は私が悪かったです。すみません。
examplePolite.english: This was my fault. I'm sorry.

notes: Men often say 'ore ga warukatta'. Stronger than plain 'gomen' because it admits fault.

english: we're in the same boat; no need to thank me
use: Your reply when someone thanks you or apologizes for a favour: we all help each other, so don't worry.

example.romaji: Ki ni shinaide. Otagaisama da yo.
example.ja: 気にしないで。お互い様だよ。
example.english: Don't worry about it. We all help each other out.

examplePolite.romaji: Iie, komatta toki wa otagaisama desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: いいえ、困った時はお互い様ですよ。
examplePolite.english: Not at all, we all need help sometimes.

notes: Also said when both sides share the blame or the hardship: 'it's the same for both of us'.

politeJa: つい〜してしまいました
english: I couldn't help it; I ended up doing it without meaning to
use: Put tsui before a verb in -chatta to admit something you did on impulse: 'tsui tabechatta'.

example.romaji: Gomen, keeki tsui zenbu tabechatta.
example.ja: ごめん、ケーキつい全部食べちゃった。
example.english: Sorry, I couldn't help eating all the cake.

examplePolite.romaji: Seeru de tsui kaisugite shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: セールでつい買いすぎてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I ended up buying too much at the sale.

notes: Tsui adds 'without meaning to'; -chatta alone already sounds a little regretful. Often said with a sheepish laugh.

use: Asked when someone mentions a person you can't place.

example.romaji: E, 'senpai' tte dare no koto?
example.ja: え、「先輩」って誰のこと？
example.english: Wait, who do you mean by 'senpai'?

examplePolite.romaji: Sumimasen, sore wa dare no koto desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、それは誰のことですか？
examplePolite.english: Sorry, who do you mean?

notes: 'Nan no koto?' is the same question for things: 'what do you mean?'.

src: ごめん、聞いてなかった
ja: ごめん、聞いてなかった
kana: ごめん、きいてなかった
politeJa: すみません、聞いていませんでした
use: Own up when you zoned out, then ask them to repeat with 'mou ikkai itte'.

example.romaji: Gomen, kiitenakatta. Mou ikkai itte?
example.ja: ごめん、聞いてなかった。もう一回言って？
example.english: Sorry, I wasn't listening. Say that again?

examplePolite.romaji: Sumimasen, kiite imasen deshita. Mou ichido onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、聞いていませんでした。もう一度お願いします。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I wasn't listening. Could you say it once more?

notes: Kiitenakatta can also mean 'nobody told me': 'sonna no kiitenakatta' is 'I wasn't told that'.

politeJa: ちょっと違うかもしれません
use: A soft way to say someone's guess or summary is off, or to correct your own word.

example.romaji: Un, demo chotto chigau kana.
example.ja: うん、でもちょっと違うかな。
example.english: Yeah, but not quite, I think.

examplePolite.romaji: Sore wa chotto chigau kamo shiremasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: それはちょっと違うかもしれませんね。
examplePolite.english: That might not be quite right.

notes: A flat 'chigau' (wrong) to someone's face sounds harsh; chotto and kana soften it.

english: is that right?; did I get it right?
use: Checks your guess, answer, route or pronunciation; the answer is 'atteru yo' (right) or 'chotto chigau' (not quite).

example.romaji: Kono michi de atteru?
example.ja: この道で合ってる？
example.english: Is this the right way?

examplePolite.romaji: Kono hatsuon de atte imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: この発音で合っていますか？
examplePolite.english: Is my pronunciation right?

notes: 'X de atteru?' = 'is X right?'. Also used for fit: 'saizu atteru' (the size fits).

use: Muttered while you try to recall something you knew, or asked so the listener reminds you.

example.romaji: Ano mise no namae, nan dakke?
example.ja: あの店の名前、何だっけ？
example.english: What was that shop called again?

examplePolite.romaji: Sumimasen, onamae wa nan deshitakke?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、お名前は何でしたっけ？
examplePolite.english: Sorry, what was your name again?

notes: -kke turns a question into 'remind me': 'itsu dakke?' (when was it again?).

english: if I remember right; I'm pretty sure
use: Put it at the start to flag that you're going from memory and might be slightly off.

example.romaji: Tashika raishuu no kayoubi datta yo.
example.ja: 確か来週の火曜日だったよ。
example.english: If I remember right, it's next Tuesday.

examplePolite.romaji: Tashika sangatsu ni hikkoshita to omoimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 確か三月に引っ越したと思います。
examplePolite.english: I'm pretty sure they moved in March.

notes: 'Tashika ni' is a different use: 'true, good point'. 'Tashika na' means 'certain, reliable'.

kana: よくおぼえてないけど
polite: yoku oboete inai n desu kedo
politeJa: よく覚えていないんですけど
use: Hedges before a fuzzy memory so you're not held to the details.

example.romaji: Yoku oboetenai kedo, tabun gonen mae kana.
example.ja: よく覚えてないけど、たぶん五年前かな。
example.english: I don't remember exactly, but maybe five years ago.

examplePolite.romaji: Yoku oboete inai n desu kedo, tashika eki no chikaku deshita.
examplePolite.ja: よく覚えていないんですけど、確か駅の近くでした。
examplePolite.english: I don't remember well, but I think it was near the station.

notes: Oboeteru = 'remember (still have in mind)'; plain oboeru means 'to learn, memorize'.

use: Opens a reflection on the past, often a mild regret or a late realization.

example.romaji: Ima omoeba, ano toki yamete yokatta.
example.ja: 今思えば、あの時やめてよかった。
example.english: Looking back, I'm glad I quit back then.

examplePolite.romaji: Ima omoeba, ii keiken deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 今思えば、いい経験でした。
examplePolite.english: Looking back, it was a good experience.

politeJa: 何て言うんでしたっけ
english: what's the word for it again?
use: Say it out loud while you hunt for a word; people will often jump in and supply it.

example.romaji: Are, nante iu n dakke? Kasa no chiisai yatsu.
example.ja: あれ、何て言うんだっけ？傘の小さいやつ。
example.english: What's it called again? The little umbrella thing.

examplePolite.romaji: Kore, nihongo de nante iu n deshitakke?
examplePolite.ja: これ、日本語で何て言うんでしたっけ？
examplePolite.english: What's this called in Japanese again?

notes: Without -kke, 'nihongo de nante iu?' simply asks how to say something in Japanese.

politeJa: 言いたいことわかりますか？
use: Checks that a clumsy explanation landed; the answer is 'un, wakaru wakaru' if it did.

example.romaji: Umaku ienai kedo, iitai koto wakaru?
example.ja: うまく言えないけど、言いたいことわかる？
example.english: I can't put it well, but you know what I mean?

examplePolite.romaji: Setsumei ga heta desu kedo, iitai koto wakarimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 説明が下手ですけど、言いたいことわかりますか？
examplePolite.english: I'm bad at explaining, but do you see what I mean?

notes: Said sharply in an argument, it becomes a challenge: 'do you get it?'.

use: Fills the gap while a word escapes you and invites the listener to guess; often repeated: 'hora, are, are!'.

example.romaji: Hora, are da yo, are! Ano akai yatsu.
example.ja: ほら、あれだよ、あれ！あの赤いやつ。
example.english: You know, that thing! The red one.

examplePolite.romaji: Hora, are desu yo. Ano yuumei na mise.
examplePolite.ja: ほら、あれですよ。あの有名な店。
examplePolite.english: You know, that one. That famous shop.

notes: 'Are da yo, are' is the same move. Hora alone also means 'look!' or 'see?'.

english: in English it's...; in English you'd say...
use: Falls back on English when you can't find the Japanese; people will often teach you the word.

example.romaji: Eigo de iu to 'deadline' na n da kedo...
example.ja: 英語で言うと「deadline」なんだけど…
example.english: In English it's 'deadline', but...

examplePolite.romaji: Eigo de iu to 'deadline' desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 英語で言うと「deadline」ですね。
examplePolite.english: In English you'd say 'deadline'.

notes: 'Eigo de nante iu?' asks the reverse: 'what's that in English?'.

use: Opens gossip or news, often as 'nee, kiita?'; say 'e, nani?' to get the rest.

example.romaji: Nee, kiita? Tanaka-san, kekkon suru n da tte.
example.ja: ねえ、聞いた？田中さん、結婚するんだって。
example.english: Hey, did you hear? Tanaka's getting married.

examplePolite.romaji: Ano nyuusu, mou kikimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: あのニュース、もう聞きましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you heard the news yet?

notes: Kiku also means 'to ask': 'sensei ni kiita?' is 'did you ask the teacher?'.

use: Shares a surprising fact or bit of trivia; the reply is 'shiranakatta!' (I had no idea) or 'shitteta' (I knew).

example.romaji: Shitteta? Ano mise, raigetsu shimaru n da yo.
example.ja: 知ってた？あの店、来月閉まるんだよ。
example.english: Did you know? That shop's closing next month.

examplePolite.romaji: Kore, shitte imashita ka? Kekkou yuumei desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: これ、知っていましたか？けっこう有名ですよ。
examplePolite.english: Did you know about this? It's pretty well known.

notes: Past shitteta is 'did you know (before I told you)'; 'shitteru?' asks 'do you know it?'.

use: Checks before sharing news so you don't repeat yourself; they'll say 'kiitenai' (you didn't) or 'kiita yo' (you did).

example.romaji: Atarashii shigoto kimatta no, mou ittakke?
example.ja: 新しい仕事決まったの、もう言ったっけ？
example.english: Did I tell you I got a new job?

examplePolite.romaji: Raigetsu hikkosu koto, mou iimashitakke?
examplePolite.ja: 来月引っ越すこと、もう言いましたっけ？
examplePolite.english: Did I mention I'm moving next month?

notes: Itta (said) and itta (went) sound the same; context tells them apart.
